input.question: How does an extended release pill work?
input.ground_truth: Many years ago they coated tiny starch balls with the drug by rolling them in a cement mixer and spraying the drug onto the balls. They spray a coat, let it dry, and then spray on a coat of shellac. They let that coat dry, and then spray on another coat of the drug; let it dry; then another coat of shellac. They put the finished tiny balls inside of a capsule. When you swallow it, the capsule opens, the balls go into your stomach, and the first coat of shellac comes off. Then the coating of drug is released, then the next coat of shellac, then the next layer of drug. These were the tiny time pills in a contact capsule. Now they make a tablet so it is like a sponge. When you swallow it, is does not fall apart. It kinda of stays together and the drug "leaks" out

Okay! Imagine you have a big chocolate bar, but you don’t want to eat it all at once. You want to eat a little bit of it every hour so you stay happy for a long time.

An extended release pill is like that big chocolate bar, but it’s medicine. The pill is made in a special way so that your body doesn’t let all the medicine out at once. Instead, it lets a little bit of the medicine out slowly, over a long time. This way, you only have to take the pill once, but the medicine works for many hours.

So, the pill is like a slow candy that gives you medicine bit by bit!
